item.title: Sri Lanka court convicts 15 men over deadly Easter Sunday bombings
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqy7z275yx65o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sri Lanka court convicts 15 men over deadly Easter Sunday bombings - Published Sri Lanka's High Court has convicted 15 men who had been charged with plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500. Those found guilty include Naufer Moulavi, who prosecutors said masterminded the suicide bombings. Nine other men were acquitted. The co-ordinated blasts at three churches and three luxury hotels were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Forty-five foreigners were among the dead. All the bombers who carried out the attacks died in the blasts. Investigators have previously blamed the bombings on Islamist extremists, and the 25 men indicted were from Sri Lanka's Muslim minority. One died in custody. The court session was adjourned before sentencing. The accused, who had been charged with more than 23,000 offences, were handcuffed in pairs and brought to the High Court in the capital Colombo in two prison buses. Most of those killed were Sri Lankans, many of whom were children. They included celebrity chef Shantha Mayadunne and her daughter, an entire young family of five, at least eight members of staff from the hotels targeted and five members of the same family from the western Sri Lankan city of Negombo. The foreigners who died included 11 Indians, eight Britons and five Americans. Among the dead there were also citizens of Australia, Bangladesh, China, Denmark, Japan, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey. Three of Danish billionaire Anders Holch Povlsen's children died in the attack on the Shangri-La hotel, while the family had been holidaying there. 'Intelligence lapse' In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities. In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks. Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions. For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks. The verdict comes as a separate investigation into former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists. The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics. Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations. Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations. - Published6 hours ago - Published21 April 2025

item.title: Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5yw8npxzrlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC - Published Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace. He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams. Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Nato is thought to have several thousand troops stationed in the Baltic state, including US and German forces. Although the US is currently reviewing its deployments in Europe, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda said on Tuesday that a new US troop rotation was on its way to his country. Sinkevičius told the BBC. "We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly." "We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us." Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat". Last week Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace. Lithuania has experienced numerous incidents in the past year, which it describes as "hybrid attacks" and blames on neighbouring Belarus, a close Russian ally. Late on Monday night, flights were disrupted at Lithuania's main airport in the capital Vilnius, because of what the airports operator called a "hybrid attack carried out by Belarus", involving objects that appeared to resemble the shape of balloons. The president's chief adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said on Tuesday it was unclear whether the objects were balloons. Nato said that as of December last year it had more than 5,000 troops in Lithuania, but says now that it is unable to give a precise figure for the numbers stationed there. Germany - a fellow Nato ally - has pledged to send a 5,000-strong combat-ready brigade to Lithuania permanently as a response to the changing security situation in Europe. However, Nato said on Tuesday it would reach "full operational capability" by the end of 2027. The Germany military has failed to recruit enough personnel voluntarily and is now turning to compulsory assignments to fill some positions. The majority of troops will be based in Rūdninkai, near the Suwałki Gap - a line that borders Lithuania and Poland and also links Belarus with Russia's Kaliningrad. The origins of last week's drone incident over Lithuania have not been confirmed, however Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it had come from the direction of Belarus. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace. "We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory." Moscow did not comment on the incident. Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine. Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel. Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year. Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones. Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one Nato member shall be considered an attack against all members". item.title: Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/cmvgy4nv9d62o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Developing El Niño becomes strongest on record weeks before expected peak - Published The developing El Niño climate phenomenon is now the strongest on record, according to scientists monitoring Pacific Ocean temperatures. Daily sea surface temperatures in a key region of the central-eastern Pacific were 3.05C above average on 19 September - exceeding the previous record of 3.02C set during the very strong El Niño of 2015. Some longer-term measures of El Niño have not yet hit record levels but this is likely to change, with the peak not expected until later this year. El Niño can cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, with the Met Office saying many of the expected impacts are already being felt. - El Niño set to be 'strongest in living memory', says Met Office - Published21 August - What is El Niño and why could it mean record temperatures? - Published11 June What is El Niño and how is it measured? El Niño is a naturally-occurring pattern, which happens about every two to seven years and tends to last for around a year. Trade winds that typically blow from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to spread eastwards. Heat is then released from the ocean into the atmosphere which can boost global temperatures and drive changes in weather patterns around the world. Forecasters track the development of El Niño by watching temperatures in a key region of the Pacific Ocean. When these are consistently 0.5C above normal, an El Niño is declared. There are different ways of measuring the strength of El Niño, however. The records that have now been broken relate to daily measurements of sea surface temperature compared with the long term historical average. This is called the Oceanic Niño Index (ONI). Many scientists - including forecasters in the USA and Australia - also consider an alternative measure known as the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI). This measures how warm the key El Niño region is relative to the rest of the tropical oceans, meaning it takes into account the background warming caused by climate change. By the RONI index the current El Niño is not yet a record-breaker - but it is likely that more announcements will follow in the coming weeks. Professor Adam Scaife, Head of Long Range Prediction at the Met Office, said: "We have been signalling for months that the developing El Niño will be an unprecedented event. "The fact that it has already exceeded previous records – with several weeks to go before it peaks later this year – shows the enormity of this El Niño." Impacts of El Niño already being felt globally Every El Niño is different, therefore impacts on global weather patterns are not guaranteed. And the unprecedented strength of this El Niño does not necessarily mean it will have unprecedented impacts on the weather. Professor Scaife said: "Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide." El Niño increases the odds of storms and floods in some regions and of drought and wildfires in others. El Niño years tend to bring below-average monsoon rainfall in India, which is already being reflected in this year's data. Statistics from the India Meteorological Department show that, until 22 September the southwest monsoon had brought 15% less rain than normal. Another typical impact of El Niño is reduced hurricane activity in the Atlantic due to changes in wind patterns high in the atmosphere. So far in 2026 there have been no Atlantic hurricanes, setting a new record for the latest date without a hurricane forming since satellite monitoring of storms began. Other possible effects - some of which are already being felt - include the increased risk of floods in coastal parts of Ecuador, Peru and the southern USA, and the enhanced threat of drought and wildfires in Brazil, Australia and Indonesia. These weather impacts can have significant knock on effects for on crop yields, food security and economies around the globe. Will there be an impact on UK weather? The UK is thousands of miles from the tropical Pacific and so the effects of El Niño tend to be less clear-cut than in other regions. However, it does bring the increased chance of wet and stormy conditions across north-west Europe during the late autumn and early winter. A forecast released by the Met Office this autumn stated that there were already "signals for increased rainfall and storminess in autumn here in the UK", especially into November and December. The winter of 2015 and 2016, which coincided with a very strong El Niño, brought a succession of major storms delivering what experts at the time described as the most extreme flooding on record. In addition to storminess, El Niño can also be associated with UK cold spells in the late winter - but the link is not a strong one and the past evidence is mixed. The so-called Big Freeze of winter 2009/2010 was, at the time, the coldest in three decades - and this coincided with an El Niño. However, 2006/2007 was also an El Niño winter and that was unseasonably warm. As this unprecedented El Niño approaches its likely peak towards the end of 2026, scientists will continue to monitor its development - and its impact on weather around the world. - Published3 September - Published7 days ago - Published1 September

item.title: Eleven injured in shooting outside Turkish school
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y0z4gv0le4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Eleven injured in shooting outside Turkish school - Published Eleven people have been injured in a shooting outside a high school in Turkey, with police detaining a 15-year-old male suspect. Two people were left in critical conditions after a gunman opened fire before fleeing on Tuesday morning, It happened at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the western province of Manisa, with the injured reportedly all students. The suspect's mother, father, and grandfather - who reportedly owned the weapon - have also been detained, according to the country's justice minister Akın Gürlek. It is the third school shooting in Turkey this year and comes as the government continues to grapple with how to address the recent spate of violence. CCTV footage appeared to show the suspect walking through empty streets checking a shotgun, which is clearly visible. He is casually dressed and appears unhurried. Later footage showed the apparent suspect, who is reportedly a student at the school, running from the scene with the weapon still in hand. The motive behind the attack was not immediately clear. According to Turkish law, the teenager is required to appear before a court before being officially arrested. In a statement, Turkey's education ministry said the incident had "deeply saddened our nation, and our educational community in particular". It said that three national investigators from the ministry had been sent to Manisa. Two deadly school shootings in April caused outrage in Turkey and led to new security measures for the 2026-2027 academic year, including tighter gun controls. Before then, the country did not have a history of school shootings. In an attack in Kahramanmaras, a 14-year-old killed nine students aged 10 and 11, and one teacher. The gunman died at the scene. - Published16 April

item.title: Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate juror and check his phone
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4gvyw80dp2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Lindsay Clancy's lawyer asks judge to investigate juror and check his phone - Published The defence lawyer for a Massachusetts mother accused of murdering her three children has asked a judge to investigate a juror in the case. The proceedings against Lindsay Clancy ended in a mistrial and acrimony this month after the jury failed to reach a unanimous verdict. Her attorney, Kevin Reddington, wants the court to probe mobile phone use by "Juror Doe" during deliberations as well as a questionnaire he filled out. A lawyer for Michael Desronvil, the lone juror who wanted to find Clancy guilty, said the latest defence motion was a "Looney Tunes" attack on his client for doing his civic duty. Desronvil has said there was "enough proof that she [Clancy] knew exactly what she was doing". Warning: This article contains distressing details The juror forewoman has claimed in a media interview that Desronvil had expressed reasonable doubt about Clancy's guilt, which would require him to find her not guilty. He denies this. Clancy has not denied killing her three children, Cora, five, Dawson, three, and Callan, eight months, at the family's Massachusetts home. Her attorneys argued she was not guilty by reason of insanity, that she was struggling with postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors said Clancy made a calculated decision to send her husband out of the house on an errand so she could strangle her children. In his motion filed on Friday, Reddington asked the court to look at calls and texts that "Juror Doe" made between 08:00 and 16:30 local time during all the days the jury deliberated. He also asked the court to examine the truthfulness of the answers the juror gave during the jury selection process, as well as his responses to prospective juror questionnaires. In a separate motion, Reddington also asked for the case against Clancy to be dismissed. Prosecutors have yet to say whether they will retry her. Facing a backlash for refusing to acquit Clancy, Desronvil has hired an attorney to represent him. The lawyer, Edward Paltzik, said in a statement on X that the "disgusting" defence motion was an attack on the US constitutional right to a fair trial. "If the new normal is that jurors are going to face brutal reprisals for disagreeing with a defense attorney, you can kiss the Sixth Amendment goodbye," he wrote. Several jurors have said after the trial ended that they were ultimately divided 11-1 in favour of finding Clancy not criminally responsible. Desronvil said last week that he had no doubt about her guilt. "As I tried to explain different possible theories during deliberation, I kept getting cut off as if I had doubts based on the evidence presented," he said in a statement to the BBC's US partner CBS News. The jury forewoman, a retired fifth-grade teacher, said in an interview with NBC that Desronvil had admitted he had reasonable doubt, but refused to find Clancy not guilty by reason of insanity.

item.title: Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from a drug overdose
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crn45d8dd2wdo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Autopsy shows Hayden Panettiere died from a drug overdose - Published Child star Hayden Panettiere died from the toxic effects of fentanyl, Xanax and several other drugs in her system, according to an autopsy completed by the Greenville County Coroner's Office in South Carolina. The coroner's office said Panettiere's death was an accident and that no signs of trauma were discovered that would have contributed to her death. Panettiere died last month at the age of 36 after she was found unresponsive at a South Carolina residence. The star of US TV shows Heroes and Nashville had spoken openly about her struggles with substance abuse. The coroner's office also found methocarbamol - a prescription muscle relaxant - and quetiapine - an antipsychotic medication that is used to treat certain mental health conditions. Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid that has killed hundreds of thousands of Americans over the past five years alone. The coroner's office said emergency responders had "initiated advanced cardiac life support measures; however, resuscitation efforts were unsuccessful". The US Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) was reportedly joining the local police department's investigation into the child star's death. Panettiere's ex-boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report from the day she died. Just months before her death, Panettiere published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction and postpartum depression. Panettiere has said she was introduced to drugs around the age of 16 during a red carpet appearance for Heroes when a member of her professional team gave her something called a "happy pill" for energy. "I had no idea that this was not an appropriate thing, or what door that would open for me when it came to my addiction," she told People Magazine. "As I got older, the drugs and alcohol became something I almost couldn't live without." Panettiere's brother, Jansen, died aged 28 from a heart condition. Panettiere revealed in her book that her brother also struggled with substance abuse and used heroin and cocaine leading up to his death. Related topics - Published17 August

item.title: Veteran BBC Africa correspondent Mark Doyle dies aged 67
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq986214den3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Veteran BBC Africa correspondent Mark Doyle dies aged 67 - Published British journalist Mark Doyle, best known for his reporting on conflicts in Africa in the 1990s and 2000s, has died aged 67 after a short illness. After living in Africa, he joined the BBC in 1986. Doyle became East Africa correspondent in 1993 and made his mark covering the Rwandan genocide a year later. As West Africa correspondent from 1997 to 2002, he reported on Sierra Leone's brutal civil war and aftermath of Liberia's conflict. Following Doyle's death, BBC foreign editor Paul Danahar said he was a "legendary figure", as well as a" brilliant, brave, empathetic reporter". The BBC's Andrew Harding, who worked with Doyle, paid tribute to his former colleague in a 2015 article, published to mark his departure from the national broadcaster. In the piece Fergal Keane, another prominent BBC correspondent in Africa, recalled their stint in Rwanda in 1994. "He stayed longer than any of us," Keane said of Doyle. "Those who were in that awful place at that awful time will know what Mark Doyle gave for the cause of truth and for the BBC." In the same article Sir David Richards, who headed British forces struggling to stop Sierra Leone's civil war in 2000, also praised Doyle. Sir David said his reporting helped convince the UK government of the need for a robust intervention. "Hence the saving of thousands of Sierra Leonean lives that would otherwise have been at huge risk," he said. In 2004 Doyle won first prize in the UN Correspondents Association/UN Foundation Awards for his coverage of post-war Liberia. He became BBC World Affairs correspondent before retiring from the BBC in 2015. - The man admired by presidents and warlords - Published29 March 2015 Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent. item.title: Iran must stop arming Houthis in Yemen, G7 says ahead of UN General Assembly
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwm2qpmepmlzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Iran must stop arming Houthis in Yemen, G7 says ahead of UN General Assembly - Published Iran must "end its arming of and support" for the Houthis in Yemen, the foreign ministers of G7 nations have said in a joint statement. The G7 also condemned "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, adding that the recent escalation in fighting against Saudi-backed pro-government forces in Yemen represented a threat to regional and global energy security. Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after the Iran-backed group seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the gateway to a key global shipping route. Iran has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically. - Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles - Published2 days ago The G7 statement comes ahead of the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to speak. "We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith," said the foreign ministers of the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. It went on: "Their reprehensible actions constitute a dangerous pattern of escalation that risks further exacerbating the conflict, undermining international trade and creating global economic instability." "Looking forward, we will continue to support the legitimate Government of Yemen and reaffirm our strong commitment to the unity, sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Yemen," the ministers said. Their statement was issued following a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. Meanwhile, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of targeting civilians in Yemen in its air strikes across the group's territory. Houth-run Saba news agency reported that a pre-dawn strike on a house in the Red Sea port city of Mokha on Tuesday killed six people, including two children and a woman. Saba also said that nine detainees were killed in an attack on a prison in al-Hazm, in Jawf province, on Monday night. The Houthis' health ministry said two members of one family were killed in a strike on Jawf province on Monday, and that one person was killed in Taiz. The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government has not yet commented. Meanwhile, government-run media reported that civilians were injured in a Houthi missile attack on a market in the Mudaribah wa al-Ara district of Lahj province, about 20km (12 miles) east of Houthi-controlled territory. Verified CCTV footage showed a munition hitting an area crowded with people and vehicles, causing a large explosion. People flee as the air is filled with dust and smoke. There was no immediate comment from the Houthis. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Earlier this month, the Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen, took control of Bab al-Mandab, a narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. Saudi Arabia has retaliated with hundreds of air strikes in the region. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia, including the capital city, Riyadh. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, involving a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Burnham said the announcement followed a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. A diplomatic source told AFP that France has pledged support as well, and says is ready to work on "securing" Saudi energy infrastructure via a "strictly defensive approach". Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also requested military support from President Donald Trump, US media reported. Trump has wavered for weeks over whether to act on a Saudi request for help in fighting the Houthis, the New York Times reported on Monday. The US president had earlier told Fox News that he was in "deciding mode" as he considered options for the next steps in the war against Iran. On Sunday, US embassies across the Middle East issued new security alerts as fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed coalition in Yemen intensified. The Houthis declare themselves to be part of the Iranian-led "axis of resistance" against Israel, the US and the wider West - along with armed group such as Hamas and Lebanon's Hezbollah movement. Although Iran has denied arming the Houthis in violation of a UN embargo, the UK and other Western powers have said their naval forces have repeatedly intercepted Iranian weapons shipments bound for Yemen during the civil war. A panel of UN experts also concluded in 2024 that the Houthis had been transformed into a powerful military organisation due to the transfer of materiel, assistance and training from Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Hezbollah and Iraqi specialists. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. Since taking control of Bab al-Mandab, they have said they pose no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

item.title: Outrage in India over viral video of teen molested and her friend beaten
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmz6z2vx65jeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Outrage in India over viral video of teen molested and her friend beaten - Published A video showing a teenaged girl being sexually assaulted and her male friend beaten by a group of men in India's Bihar state has sparked widespread outrage. The school students, both minors, were stopped in Jamui district on 19 September. Footage shared widely online shows them surrounded and repeatedly pleading to be allowed to leave. The boy is seen being slapped and pulled by his collar, while the girl is touched inappropriately and, in another clip, carried away by a man as the boy tries to intervene. Three accused, also minors, have been arrested in connection with the assault. A special investigation team has been set up to catch the other suspects. The disturbing footage has prompted anger over the harassment of the two teenagers and renewed a wider debate about the safety of women and girls in Bihar, as well as questions over the response of state authorities. The outrage intensified after Bihar minister Shravan Kumar said that "sporadic incidents keep happening" and that the government was keeping a watch on them. "The world is not entirely free of crime," he said, adding that those responsible would not be allowed to escape and would face strict action. Umesh Kushwaha, of the governing Janata Dal (United), also faced criticism after referring to such cases as "isolated incidents" and contrasting the government's record with that of the previous RJD administration. Kushwaha later said his remarks had been "distorted and misrepresented" and promised action against those responsible. Police said the incident took place around 19:00 local time [13:30 GMT] on Saturday, but it came to light on Monday after the video of the assault went viral. The teenagers, both students of 10th standard, attended the same coaching institute and had gone to the area to take photographs after their classes, according to police. Jamui police chief Bishwajeet Dayal said neither of them had initially reported the incident - officers began investigating after the video circulated widely online and traced the pair using the registration number of a vehicle visible in the footage. Their statements were subsequently recorded and a case was registered following a written complaint from the girl. A case has been registered under India's stringent Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, or Pocso. Police have also invoked sections of India's criminal code covering assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, assault or criminal force with intent to disrobe, and acts carried out with a common intention. Senior police officer KS Anupam said three minors had been arrested and that investigators had established the involvement of two other people. Police have also begun action against 32 social media accounts accused of circulating footage in which the teenagers could be identified, she added. The shocking nature of the assault has provoked outrage online, with many social media users expressing horror and questioning why a group of men believed they had the right to confront two teenagers for being together. Some characterised the incident as an extreme form of "moral policing", while others tagged Bihar police and demanded strict action against the harassers. Shreyasi Singh, a Bihar minister and legislator from Jamui, told NDTV news channel, external the incident had brought "shame to society". Singh, a former international-level sport shooter, said women in Bihar were advancing in many areas but concerns about their safety persisted. She called for the remaining suspects to be arrested quickly and for strict action against those responsible. Opposition leaders, meanwhile, have seized on the case to question the state government's record on women's safety. Rahul Gandhi, MP and senior leader of India's main opposition Congress party, described the footage as "deeply disturbing" and said the incident reflected a patriarchal "belief that men could police a girl's body, movements and choices". "This is not culture. It is patriarchy," Gandhi wrote on X (formerly Twitter). Tejashwi Yadav, the opposition leader in Bihar, said the incident had left him "deeply ashamed" and accused the government of failing to ensure the safety of women and girls in the state. Members of Bihar's governing coalition have rejected the opposition's wider criticism of the state's law-and-order record and said those responsible for the attack would face strict action. India's National Commission for Women has also intervened, calling for all those involved to be identified and arrested and for an impartial investigation. The commission has asked for a report from Bihar police and urged authorities to prevent further sharing of the video clips to protect the girl's identity and privacy. The Bihar State Women's Commission has also sought information from district authorities about the action being taken in the case.

item.title: Doctor in court to face Rwanda genocide charges in UK
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6790y1gj247o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Doctor in court to face Rwanda genocide charges - Published A 65-year-old doctor has appeared in court, the first person in the UK to be charged over the genocide in Rwanda in 1994. Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, who is in custody, confirmed his name and address from the dock at Westminster Magistrates' Court. He was charged following a seven year British investigation into the killings. He was told he faced a charge of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder, as a crime against humanity. The case was passed to the Old Bailey for a hearing on 9 October. A bail application will be considered later on Tuesday. The 1994 killings in Rwanda lasted 100 days, during which Hutu extremists carried out a campaign of slaughter against Tutsis and other moderate Hutus. The charges against Brown relate to an alleged slaughter in the Rugenge district of Kigali between 6 April and 13 April in 1994. Brown is accused of "killing, directing or encouraging" the deaths of members of the Tutsi ethnic group, as well as intending to destroy the group "as a whole or in part." Prosecutors said he was being charged with genocide under the 2001 International Criminal Court Act and the alleged killings were "part of a widespread or systematic attack, directed against a civilian population, with knowledge of the attack." Three members of the same house were allegedly murdered, along with a taxi driver, a mother and her young son. The alleged victims were Dominique Mukurarinda, Immaculee Mukankusi, Gerasi Rurangirwa, Leandre Mbogoye, Charlotte Kamaguja and Olivier Tuyishime. Brown is a medical doctor who qualified in Rwanda in the 1980s. He later became head of the country's Department of Family Health in Kigali and lived in a suburb there with his wife and young son. In 2006 he was worked at Praxis, a London-based charity which helps refugees from places like Rwanda. He has also served on the Refugee Nurses Task Force, which was set up in 2003 to advise the UK government. Senior police officers have previously stressed the UK should not be a safe haven for alleged war criminals, and investigators have been trained in international war crimes legislation. Sam Blom-Cooper, a barrister for Brown, told the court his client denied the allegations and was intent on going in front of a jury to clear the "stains of these appalling allegations." He said the defendant had hoped for, longed for, and prayed for the best part of 20 years, for this day." "These are appalling crimes, terrible murders committed in 1994 but this is the beginning of the end for Dr Brown." Inquiries continue into other alleged genocide offences in Rwanda.

item.title: Four dead after powerful Typhoon Dujuan lashes Japan
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3wj2lexl97o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Four dead after powerful Typhoon Dujuan lashes Japan - Published Four people have died in Japan after Typhoon Dujuan battered Tokyo and surrounding prefectures with torrential rains and destructive winds, local reports said. The storm cut power for 50,000 people and caused the suspension of hundreds of flights. Most evacuation orders were lifted on Tueday as the storm pulled away from Japan's eastern coast. At the height of the storm on Monday, authorities warned of an "imminent threat to life" and urged 1.9 million people to move to shelters. The fatalities were from landslides in Kanagawa and Chiba prefectures. Six others were reported missing, public broadcaster NHK reported. Dujuan had sustained winds of 130km/h (81mph) and gusts of 194km/h. The typhoon is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", which has warmed the ocean, fuelling the formation of storms. Authorities had advised the public to pay attention to weather information. Dujuan, which is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year, hit in the midst of a five-day holiday and forced the cancellation of several events. Concerts scheduled for Monday at the Rock in Japan music festival were cancelled, while the Tokyo Game Show, a video game convention, also cancelled Monday's programme. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi offered her condolences in a post on X to those who lost their lives in the typhoon, before saying she would be continuing with her scheduled trip the United States as planned. "With a sense of urgency, I instructed Chief Cabinet Secretary Takehara and Minister Hosono to respond with utmost preparedness," she wrote, before saying she had boarded a flight to the US. She will be speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, and will meet with US President Donald Trump. The Yokosuka City Fire Department told the BBC that a woman in Kanagawa prefecture, aged in her 60s, was believed to have been buried alive after a landslide swept the house she lived in. Following a search by rescue crews, she was found inside the home and pronounced dead, NHK reported. Separately, Sodegaura City Fire Department in Chiba prefecture told the BBC a man in his 50s was rescued after getting trapped while working to clear debris at a landslide site. The department said the worker fell into a bamboo thicket, along with some heavy machinery. He was then taken to hospital before his death was confirmed, according to local reports. Police are investigating the details of the incident. Some research suggests that Japan has become more exposed to destructive storms, but climate change is not thought to be increasing the number of these storms globally, and could even make them less common in some regions. As temperatures rise, typhoons that do form are likely to become more intense on average, however. Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds. And because a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, these storms could also bring heavier rainfall. This year, El Niño - the natural weather phenomenon bringing warmer water to parts of the tropical Pacific - is another factor. El Niño doesn't have a clear effect on the total number of typhoons, but it can affect where typhoons form, their strength and which countries they hit. Some El Niño events may expose Japan to stronger typhoons, for example. The typhoon is continuing to travel along the country's Pacific coast, heading north. The extent of the damage today may not be known until Tuesday. Additional reporting by Chie Kobayashi and Mark Poynting, climate reporter - Published11 June

Major US outlets suspend shared Trump coverage in protest at media ban - Published Major US television networks suspended their pooled coverage of President Donald Trump on Monday in response to CNN, Politico and MS NOW being barred from the White House. Trump announced the ban on Friday as he accused the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. The companies said their reporters were denied access to the building on Saturday. The three US outlets have since said they will sue the Trump administration in a bid to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports". Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president. - What is the White House press pool and why is it in a row with Trump? - Published3 hours ago Several other US outlets have also announced that they would not participate in coverage of pooled events, with some, including the New York Times and Washington Post, saying they would not share still images from Trump events on Monday. It meant there was no network TV footage of Trump boarding Air Force One or arriving in New York to attend the UN general assembly. Trump also took part in a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new Marine One helipad on the White House South Lawn. The event was streamed on the White House site but his comments were inaudible. The president did later appear on television following a meeting with the Mayor of New York Zohran Mamdani. He told the president that all members of the media would be welcome at the press conference. Trump said: "It's interesting because, they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn't very worried about that. Look at all that press." The pool involves media organisations sharing material to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public. Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds a rotating role helping to organise media TV crews covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering designated as pool coverage" of Trump. The message said the move followed the White House "preventing" CNN from fulfilling its pool duties for Trump's trip to New York and that "there will be no replacement pool put in place". The three media organisations banned from the White House filed a lawsuit on Monday in US District Court in Washington. A joint statement announcing the legal action said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." Related topics - Published15 hours ago - Published2 days ago

item.title: British man missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue teenager
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx8d38djqm25o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
British man missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue teenager - Published Italian authorities are searching for a British man who went missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue a teenager. The local coastguard said the man, in his late thirties, had been attempting to rescue two people - a father and his 16-year-old son - who were in distress in the water near the lake's western shore on Monday afternoon, local officials said. The man, who was friends with the family, had been on a boating trip with them at the time, the coastguard said. The father and son were later rescued by a passing boat, but the man has not been seen again. The UK Foreign Office said: "We are supporting the family of a British national missing in Italy and are in contact with the local authorities." A helicopter, divers and boat units from the fire department, coastguard and state police have been drafted into the search. As the lake's depth can reach more than 250m in the search area, rescuers were also preparing to deploy two underwater robots to scan the lake bed where the lake becomes too deep for divers, the Italian Coast Guard said in a statement. The alarm was first raised around 13:30 local time (12:30 BST) on Monday, when the man noticed his friend and the boy experiencing difficulty swimming and jumped in to help them. The teenager's mother, who had remained on the boat with her younger son, called the emergency services when she saw the man sinking beneath the surface. The father and son were transferred to a coastguard boat that had responded to the call and were given medical treatment after suffering from the onset of hypothermia, officials said. The mother and younger son, who were at this point adrift around 600m from shore, were then brought back to land. The coastguard earlier said that it had been the father who had jumped in to save the boy and the 37-year-old man, before revising its statement of events. Lake Como, around 30 miles north of Milan, is a popular tourist hotspot, with more than 78,000 foreign visitors in 2024, local chamber of commerce research shows. However, water temperatures there can start to fall from September onward.

item.title: Father admits causing death of his son in Cyprus hotel fall
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm4gvyz2vlkvo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Father admits causing death of his son in hotel fall - Published A British man has pleaded guilty to causing the death of his two-year-old son who fell from a hotel window in Cyprus. Joshua Foster, from Essex, admitted a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act at a court in Paphos on Tuesday. The boy fell from the fourth floor of the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas on 12 July, the Times had previously reported. A further hearing will take place on 5 October when the prosecutor will set out the facts of the case and the defence will present mitigation, a court official confirmed. Foster was allowed to return to the UK for his child's funeral, on condition that he flew back to Cyprus last week for the plea hearing to take place. His lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, said he would ask the court to lift travel restrictions so that his client can return to the UK to be with his wife and daughter until the next hearing. Paphos District Court was told in July that the boy fell through an open window when his father was holding him around his waist and swinging him from side to side. Foster decided to plead guilty to avoid a long trial and spare his family reliving the child's death in court, Alexandrou said. A long trial would mean that the man was "again a victim of this tragedy", the lawyer told the Associated Press after Tuesday's hearing. "The most important thing for him is to return to his family," he said. The maximum sentence for the charge was four years in prison, but Alexandrou said the court should take previous cases into account where defendants had been fined or received a suspended sentence. In a statement given to the BBC, Alexandrou, said: "This was a momentary lapse of attention, without any intention to cause harm, which had the most devastating and unimaginable consequences. "We will now present to the court the relevant mitigating evidence and circumstances for consideration ahead of sentencing." The family have suffered "unimaginable grief" since the "horrific events" and have asked for privacy during this time, added the lawyer.
