item.title: Texas ICE shooting leaves Venezuelan DoorDash driver with bullet in his back, says lawyer
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3y0z25v0zjwo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Texas ICE shooting leaves Venezuelan DoorDash driver with bullet in his back, says lawyer - Published A Venezuelan DoorDash delivery driver who was shot by ICE agents was transferred from hospital to a detention centre with a bullet still in his back, his lawyer has told US media. The shooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, 28, triggered protests in Austin, Texas, on Sunday. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement to the BBC it was investigating the shooting of a man in the Texan capital who had entered the country illegally. It was unclear what led to the shooting with the local mayor and police demanding an investigation. It comes months after a man in Houston was shot dead by an ICE officer. Attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told CBS that Garcés Perez called his wife while "yelling in pain" in hospital. She told National Public Radio he was in ICE custody. The Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement efforts and arrests during Trump's second term, sparking unrest across several US cities. The administration has defended its policies and the agency's controversial tactics as necessary for public safety and to enact Trump's campaign promise to secure the border and carry out mass deportations. The shooting in Austin on Sunday occurred just before 1300 local time, although details remain scarce. Dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave Austin. Local television outlets showed the demonstrators gathering across the street from a blue Toyota Corolla that sustained damage to the passenger-side door, as ICE agents stood nearby, Reuters news agency reported. Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said that Austinites have a right to know what happened and "a right to feel safe in their city" during a media briefing on Sunday. "They should know the truth," he said, adding that he is pleased that the city will also be involved in the investigation. He added that ICE operations have surged in Austin in recent weeks. ICE has faced intense scrutiny after a number of deadly shootings, including the death of Houston resident Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Salgado Araujo had not been a target of an ICE investigation, but was shot during an ICE traffic stop, according to DHS. Texas Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat, has demanded a full and immediate independent investigation into the latest shooting and the release of body camera footage. He also demanded "accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law". Activists say that the administration has violated due process as it carries out the crackdown. Democrats have demanded reforms at the agency, including requiring immigration enforcement agents to wear body cameras and not conceal their faces. Earlier this month the US Department of Justice charged an ICE agent with lying about the non-fatal shooting of a Venezuelan migrant in Minnesota - a rare instance in which the current justice department accused a federal agent of breaking the law on the job. Earlier this week, Florida lawmaker Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican who has spoken out against the immigration crackdown, released an advert criticising the targeting and detaining of individuals who have no criminal record. Salazar appeared on the CBS programme Face the Nation on Sunday and said that she has since spoken to the president, and believes he will keep the country on the right track. "He gets it more than anybody," she said. Related topics - Published4 February - Published4 September

item.title: Canadian province sues OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge school shooting
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3wyz2rkgrx0o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Canadian province sues OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge school shooting - Published A Canadian province is suing OpenAI over its alleged failure to notify authorities about concerning user interactions on ChatGPT prior to the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting. The company has previously apologised for not flagging Jessie Van Rootselaar's account to law enforcement before the 18-year-old killed eight people, including six children, in February. British Columbia attorney general Niki Sharma said the lawsuit, filed to a US federal court on Monday, raised questions about "the responsibilities of technology companies when they become aware of credible threats of serious violence". Families of those killed or injured in the shooting have filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI. Media reports revealed that Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT activity was flagged by OpenAI's safety team for references to gun violence months before the attack, but the company did not alert local authorities. In April, OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman apologised to the families of the victims. "I am deeply sorry that we did not alert law enforcement," Altman wrote in an open letter. The BBC has requested comment from OpenAI regarding the latest lawsuit. "To date, OpenAI has not taken meaningful steps to address the concerns raised by survivors, families and the Tumbler Ridge community," Sharma said in a statement. "The company still has an opportunity to demonstrate accountability by strengthening safeguards, improving transparency and taking concrete action to help prevent similar tragedies in the future." Speaking to reporters on Monday, Sharma said she had not read the contents of the OpenAI chats. "We have asked OpenAI to disclose these chats. They have refused. We should all be asking them: Why?" she said, according to CBC, external. Sharma said the lawsuit was filed in California, as the alleged decision not to report the shooter's ChatGPT account occurred in that US state, according to AFP. Sharma told reporters that any financial damages won by the province would go towards rebuilding the secondary school.

item.title: Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/ckz7z5w7ey2jo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Neutral venues and no 'away' fans - how Israel v Republic of Ireland became so contentious - Published An elite-level European football match will be played on Sunday at a neutral stadium, with no 'away' fans, and reduced television coverage. That the match is even taking place had been in doubt - one side had to vote on a motion confirming whether or not they would participate amid significant opposition from fans, pundits and politicians. But the vote confirmed the fixture would go ahead, and now the Republic of Ireland will travel to Debrecen, Hungary, for a Uefa Nations League 'away' match against Israel, played against a backdrop of ongoing and increasingly volatile disagreement between the two countries about Israel's military offensive in Gaza. And on 4 October, the Republic of Ireland will face the same opponents in a 'home' match in Backa Topola - a small town in Serbia. No tickets have been sold to Irish fans for either fixture, and Irish public broadcaster RTE will air a stripped-back version of match coverage, with no commentators, pundits, or half-time analysis. So how did a Uefa Nations League match become one of the most contentious fixtures in football? Venue changes have not quietened protests As soon as the Republic of Ireland were placed with Israel - plus Austria and Kosovo - at the Nations League draw in February, the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) faced calls from some to boycott the matches because of Israel's military action in Gaza. In May a friendly match the Republic of Ireland played against Qatar in Dublin was twice interrupted after fans threw tennis balls onto the pitch featuring the Palestinian flag. The FAI eventually took a vote of its delegates in July, in which 75 members voted to play the matches and 32 voted to boycott. Not playing the matches could have harmed Irish football in the long-run, the FAI said, amid the possibility of Uefa sanctions for refusing to fulfil the fixtures and the potential loss of millions of euros in income. As well as curtailing its coverage, RTE will not take advertising or sponsorship income from the matches, saying it will only "meet its contractual obligations" to broadcast the fixtures. No tickets are being sold to Irish fans for either the 'home' or 'away' matches, with a small allocation available for Israeli fans for the first fixture, which has been the case at multiple previous Israel home games held in Hungary. Hungary has been deemed a suitable host nation for Israel matches because the two nations enjoy stronger diplomatic ties than those between Israel and many other European nations, and it has been willing to provide the necessary policing and security arrangements for matches to operate smoothly. The FAI decided in the summer to play its 'home' fixture against Israel at a neutral stadium, citing "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil". Reports have claimed the FAI was concerned protests could prevent the match from taking place in Dublin. The FAI gave no official reason for the selection of Backa Topola, but choosing a venue in Serbia - in a town so remote - in theory renders security management easier and reduces the possibility of protest. In 2025, Serbian foreign minister Marko Duric described Israel as one of Serbia's "closest friends and strategic partners". Serbia has also purchased military equipment, including drones and missiles, from Israel in recent years. The decision to play in neutral stadiums has not curtailed opposition. Fans of various Irish clubs have demonstrated against the matches during domestic fixtures in recent weeks, and on Monday more than 160 Irish athletes signed an open letter by the Irish Sport for Palestine group urging a boycott. The signatories include boxer Tyrone McKenna and former European champion athlete Ciara Mageean. FAI CEO David Courrell said last week Uefa had rejected a request for the teams to be kept apart in future draws, director of football John Martin described the games as a "very uncomfortable situation for everyone". Manager Heimer Hallgrimsson, meanwhile, said playing the match did not constitute legitimisation of Israel's "genocide". "We're not playing with genocide, we're playing against genocide," Hallgrimmson said. "We're playing against Israel, we're not playing with Israel." In response, the Israel Football Association accused Hallgrimsson of "ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity". The Republic of Ireland faced Israel in Women's EuroBasket qualifiers last autumn and earlier this year after "extensive deliberations". Irish support for Palestinians is long-standing The Republic of Ireland has been among the European countries to most keenly show support for Palestinians since the start of Israel's military offensive in Gaza in October 2023. More than 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations (UN). In May 2024, alongside Spain and Norway, Ireland officially recognised a Palestinian state, and later that year joined South Africa's Gaza genocide case against Israel in the International Court of Justice. The country has also boycotted Eurovision since 2025 because of Israel's ongoing participation in the song contest, was the first EU country to ban goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank, and has issued travel bans for Israeli government ministers. On Monday, Irish foreign minister Helen McEntee said: "Ireland's view is clear - international law is being breached. We are seeing an attempt to erase a population." Israel has criticised Ireland's standpoint and claims its actions in Gaza constitute self-defence, after the armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages. Last summer a UN commission of inquiry found that Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, and this year a further investigation determined that the country has deliberately targeted children with military force, resulting in genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations it has committed genocide. The Republic of Ireland is not the only nation to have expressed reluctance to face Israel in international football. In 2024, Belgium refused to host Israel on home soil, and the match was held instead in Debrecen. The president of the Norwegian Football Association, Lise Klaveness, made a public statement last year saying Israel should be suspended from European competitions, and Turkey also called for Israel to be banned. In a statement released on Tuesday, Amnesty International said Uefa was "giving Israel an international stage" rather than "sending a clear message there is a cost" for its actions in Gaza. BBC Sport reported last autumn that Uefa executives were considering a vote on whether to ban Israel, under pressure from representatives from a number of nations. But any plan to hold a vote was pulled when the first phase of a ceasefire was announced last October.

item.title: What is the White House pool and why is it in a row with Trump?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dx5dy5rzz2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
What is the White House pool and why is it in a row with Trump? - Published When Donald Trump unveiled a helipad at the White House on Monday, his remarks were barely audible in live footage of the event. This was due to a row over an institution that rarely makes the news – the White House Press pool. Yet it is at the heart of relations between the US president and the media, and this dispute could have constitutional implications. Coverage of upcoming presidential engagements, which include the UN General Assembly in New York, could be affected. What is the White House press pool? It is a group of news organisations that combine resources to follow presidents wherever they are - in the Oval Office, at state dinners, on Air Force One or on holiday. There are separate pools for TV, photographers and print and radio outlets, as well as a "new media" category. The idea, conceived decades ago, is that having a pool saves on costs and space and it's not practical for hundreds of media outlets to follow the president around. Members of the pool share their material - pictures and descriptions of the president's movements - with the wider media. The pool is always on standby in case an event requires the president to speak to the nation. This latest row centres on the TV pool which has five members - CNN, ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC. It began on Friday when Trump said he was banning three outlets - CNN, Politico and MS NOW - from the White House, accusing them of spreading "fake news" and "fictions and lies" about his team. A day later, reporters from those organisations found that their entry badges to the White House had been disabled. On Monday, all the major US TV networks decided to pull out of White House pool duties - in effect boycotting presidential events. That afternoon came the first test of this post-pool era - the new helipad at the White House. With no pool cameras present, much of the media did not carry any pictures and for those that did, there was no microphone to clearly pick up the president's remarks. But there were no such problems at Trump's meeting later that day with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, because it was not dependent on pool cameras and lots of media were there. Why did US networks pull out of filming Trump? Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds the rotating role covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage" of President Trump. In a joint statement, the five networks said: "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. "No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting." The First Amendment of the US Constitution protects speech and press freedoms. It forbids the government from "abridging" the freedom of the press - language that courts have traditionally interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage. CNN, Politico and MS NOW have filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports". A hearing is scheduled for Wednesday. In a joint statement on Monday, they said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." Trump's speech to the United Nations on Tuesday will be unaffected by the boycott because it will be carried by outlets which are not part of the pool. But the president's movements to and from his various New York events, which are usually filmed, could be subject to the blackout. How has Trump reacted and what is Trump TV? Responding to news of the lawsuit, Trump called the outlets "Third Rate Clowns" and "Crooked and Corrupt Press" that "trivialise and demean" his achievements. "Fake News people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our National Security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown 'sources,' shouldn't be allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World," Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. He added that his team would file an appeal. Meanwhile the White House has launched Trump TV, a 24/7 stream on YouTube. Its description reads: "Watch the Trump Administration's biggest moments all in one place." So far, the channel has primarily consisted of replays of previous Trump speeches and rallies. For now, the White House media slot has remained vacant and instead the conservative TV outlet, Real America's Voice, was listed as "secondary" crew on Trump's trip to New York. Unlike the traditional pool, however, that outlet is under no obligation to share material with others and has operated unilaterally for its audience. Have there been previous examples of White House media bans? In February, the White House announced it was taking control of the press pool which has access to Trump and had for more than a century been managed by the White House Correspondents' Association. The same month, the administration moved to bar Associated Press reporters and photographers from spaces where access is limited, such as the Oval Office or Air Force One, because of the outlet's usage of the term "Gulf of Mexico" instead of "Gulf of America". AP filed a lawsuit and the case remains ongoing. There have been a few instances of other administrations attempting to limit certain outlets' access. The Obama administration tried to exclude Fox News from participating in a press pool interview with an administration official in 2009. But after pushback from the other four networks in the pool, Fox News was granted access. Unlike with Trump's exclusion of CNN, MS NOW and Politico, the Obama administration did not try to bar Fox News from all pool coverage, just one specific interview.

item.title: Can you take the 'London' out of London Fashion Week?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cklyjz20pd22o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Can you take the 'London' out of London Fashion Week? - Published The curtain might have fallen on London Fashion Week (LFW) - but bosses hope the runway of the future will start to look a bit different. Fashion Britain is the British Fashion Council's initiative to open up access to talent outside of London - so how do you shift the focus away from the traditional centre of that world? The council told BBC Newsbeat it has been working with LFW on a series of pop-up events in England, Wales and Scotland to show this year's event was "bigger than London". Northern Ireland wasn't included as a location for this year's initiative - but will be included next year, the council said. A recent House of Commons report, external found that more than half (51%) of the creative industries' economic output was generated in London in 2022. However, it did report that there are "clusters of creative industries" across the country, which included cities like Manchester and Leeds. "A lot of people think in order to make it big, you have come to this big city because it has the schools here," says Charles Jeffrey, founder and creative director of international fashion label Loverboy. "But actually, there is so much amazing education that happens in different places," the Scottish designer tells Newsbeat. "I first started [in] a tiny studio in Dalston [in east London] and we were having to use fabrics from these cheap fabric shops that you would probably only really get in London because of the rag trade," he recalls. "Now a lot of them have gone and what made London a capital city for fashion has been taken away, so you're probably better getting your fabrics from a little fabric shop in Manchester - it's probably ten times cheaper." Jeffrey supported Fashion Britain this year, with the aim of opening doors in the industry for creatives outside of London, but how feasible will that be? Birmingham City University graduate Imarnie Bennett knows a bit about the struggle. She travelled to the capital to showcase her project with fellow BCU fashion graduates to an audience at Somerset House. "London is such a big city, it's really well known and there are lots of opportunities," says the 22-year-old. "You hear Birmingham and it's a bit like, 'will they get us the same opportunities as London?', but I feel like Birmingham is becoming more noticed for what we do." Bennett says you can harness the power of being different. "Even colours, some cities are brighter and warmer than others, so it changes people's perspectives on things," she says. Yet fellow designer Sean Pajarillo says he is hopeful about job opportunities because of how the technology and fashion industry is moving. "The merging of industries is what's going to create new opportunities for someone in the future," says the 25-year-old. Natalie Potter is network director at the British Fashion Council, and says the Fashion Britain initiative is "about recognising that British fashion is bigger than London". Potter says that in the run up to LFW there were events in London, Bristol, Manchester, Liverpool, Newcastle, Edinburgh, Dundee and Cardiff. But what happens after the catwalk leaves town? Potter says the aim of Fashion Britain is that it will connect talent to "the infrastructure and opportunities that they need to grow". "So working with the big global businesses that we do across the country to make sure that they've got routes to retail, to give them active mentorship," she explains. Potter says this will happen "locally and regionally". This is something that British designer Priya Ahluwalia believes is vital. "I do think there is a genuine issue with London being seen as the centre of the universe in terms of fashion," she says. "There is incredible talent from all over the UK, some of the best designers have come from the north, come from Wales, Scotland". Ahluwalia spoke to Newsbeat after showcasing her archive at Westfield Stratford City shopping centre as part of Fashion Week. The designer explained how practical help is important in helping talent access the industry. "Whether we decentralise or not, London is still going to be the centre of UK fashion. "There needs to also be support for people to be able to travel to London, show up in London", Ahluwalia says. For Jeffrey, formal training isn't the only way into the fashion world. "Sometimes having a university degree does kind of put your foot in the door - but honestly, I really think it's just about the work and work ethic."

item.title: Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6vgyz1n0v1xo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability - Published Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a political record-breaker. The problem for him is these records are overwhelmingly negative and he is at risk of losing his job over them. The problem for the EU and for Europe more broadly is this has a destabilising effect far further afield. At a paltry 13%, Merz's popularity rating is the lowest for any German chancellor since polling began. German voters' ardour for him started lower and fell faster than any of his predecessors. The former corporate lawyer is perceived by many to be arrogant and out of touch with their problems. He has only been in government for 16 months but under his chairmanship, Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party has suffered three very poor showings in regional elections over the last couple of weeks. The state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern broke another record on Sunday according to preliminary results: Merz's conservative CDU party did not even reach the 5% threshold to enter the regional parliament. Conversely, the anti-immigration, nationalist right Alternative for Germany (AfD) - a political party Merz had promised to slash support for when he was running for CDU leadership - has performed spectacularly well. It became the biggest political faction in two out of those three recent state elections and broke another record: they have a chance at governing in one of those states, Saxony Anhalt, despite the German authorities labelling them in part anti-democratic and far-right extremist. The AfD also tops opinion polls nationally, a particularly sensitive issue for Germany after its Nazi past. The party rejects the far-right label. Its German name, Alternative fuer Deutschland, means Alternative for Germany. That is exactly what they say voters now want. Following this month's regional election surge in success for the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, plus its gains in Berlin - where the victors were the hard left Die Linke party - AfD co-leader Alice Weidel said on Monday that her party had effectively replaced the center-right CDU as Germany's true Volkspartei, or catch-all people's party. The AfD accuses Merz of failing to fulfil his key election promises to improve the spluttering German economy - once seen as the financial engine of Europe - and to find workable solutions to voter fears about immigration and security on their streets. High time for political change, says the AfD. Merz's position as German chancellor certainly looks wobbly. There have been rumours for weeks of a brewing palace coup, where he would be replaced by a more popular CDU politician. Possible candidate names are swirling but no individual will stick out his or her neck in public until they know they have the backing of the party. I have reported on Germany for decades. This is a stability-obsessed country. This kind of political upheaval is deeply unusual. Even if Merz stays in post, his political clout and credibility, his room for manoeuvre inside a fractious coalition government, will be restricted. Looking uncharacteristically forlorn on Sunday evening, Merz jumped to make a televised address even before the regional election results were confirmed. He would press ahead with tax, welfare and economic reforms to bring about prosperity, he said. "Backbone, steadfastness and patience" were required. But German patience is running thin. Voters in Germany, as across much of Europe, have repeatedly elected traditional parties of the centre-left, such as Germany's SPD party, or centre-right, like the CDU, since World War Two - but increasingly they feel let-down and frustrated as they fear for their economic future. Voter resentment really started to mount after the financial crisis of 2007/8, when these traditional parties were seen bailing out big banks, while families felt their savings and living standards dropped. Then came the 2015 migration crisis, when more than one million refugees and other migrants arrived by people-smuggler boats across the Mediterranean and made their way across Europe, often by foot, trying to settle in wealthier countries like Germany and Sweden. Germany took in one million people. Integration into German society has been mixed and Germans have been shocked and scared by a number of headline-making attacks by migrants over the years, some with a history of mental illness, others linked by the German authorities to Islamist extremist groups or ideology. In December, for example, police said they arrested five individuals suspected of plotting a Christmas market attack in Munich "based on an Islamist motive". Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 has had another scarring effect. Germans pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe. The loss of access to cheap Russian energy that German car factories and other industries relied on, plus Donald Trump's trade tariffs and aggressive economic competition from China, have had a heavy toll on this country's export-driven economy. Germany is Europe's, and therefore the eurozone currency's, largest economy. It is the world's largest single donor to Ukraine right now and it is the biggest net payer into the EU budget. When Germany's finances are in trouble and the country turns inward because of a political crisis, the knock-on effect beyond its borders can be considerable. Under financial pressure, Merz has been pushing hard, along with a group of other wealthier EU countries to slash their contributions to the bloc's budget, for example. This comes at a time when the EU wants to spend more, not less, on common defence projects, migration and AI and tech. Faced with perceived threats from Russia and China, wars in the Middle East affecting energy supplies and prices, plus the unpredictability - and many in Europe say, unreliability - of the US under Trump, now is a time Europeans must stick tightly together, says Brussels. The EU is watching Merz's travails, plus the strengthening of the AfD on the right and the hard left Die Linke too, with concern. These regional German votes come at the start of bumper election season across the EU, where all the big powers - (including France, Italy, Spain and Poland - go to the polls. Nationalist, Eurosceptic, anti-immigration parties are predicted to do well. And Beijing and Moscow are watching closely.

item.title: Why a Bollywood celebrity manager's 2020 death case has been reopened
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cpwl1ejlgw9o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Why a Bollywood celebrity manager's 2020 death case has been reopened - Published On 4 June 2020, as a deadly wave of Covid-19 swept through India, celebrity manager Disha Salian asked her father Satish Salian to call a police helpline to check if it was safe for her to travel. She was excited about an advertising campaign she was going to shoot and showed her parents a photo of the cheque she had received as advance remuneration. As she walked out of the door, she told her parents that she would be back in two days. It was the last time the Salians saw their 28-year-old daughter alive. On the intervening night of 8 and 9 June, Satish Salian was called by the police to a hospital where he learnt that his only child was dead. Police said she had fallen from the 12th floor of a building in the western city of Mumbai. Disha's friends at the hospital said she had been drinking alcohol and fell accidentally. Police later said their investigation had shown that her death was a suicide. But earlier this month, the Bombay High Court ordered the federal police - the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) - to reopen the case and reinvestigate Disha's death. The court order came after a petition filed last year by Satish Salian, who had insisted from the start that his daughter's death was not a suicide or an accident and alleged that she was gang-raped and murdered. His allegations that some senior police officers had destroyed evidence and created a false story of suicide to protect some ministers and influential politicians who had a role in the alleged crime has made it one of India's most discussed deaths in recent years. In the order, external on 2 September, Judges Sarang V Kotwal and Ranjitsinha Raja Bhonsale criticised the police and said there were "too many glaring discrepancies" in their investigation, which was carried out in two phases over more than six years. The judges insisted that they were not holding "a mini trial" but said "the investigation carried out by the police raises more questions than it answers". They pointed out the unexplained delay in police paperwork, that no blood had been found at the spot where the body had fallen and said that the injuries mentioned in the post-mortem report did not seem consistent with a fall. "We find this difficult to accept," they wrote. One of the biggest criticisms from the court was that the police had only investigated it as a case of suspicious or unnatural death and not registered an FIR (First Information Report) - a document police have to prepare when they receive information about a crime. Satish Salian's accusations are only allegations so far, but they have formed the basis of a new investigation by the CBI, which last week registered an FIR based on a written complaint from him. The BBC has reviewed this FIR and read through the court order in the case. Summarising Satish Salian's allegations, the court order said that at the time of her death, Disha was working with Kwan Entertainment - a celebrity management company - and represented Bollywood actor Sushant Singh Rajput. "She got to know about some objectionable activities of the powerful people. She gave that information to Rajput, who innocently divulged that to others. Ultimately that information reached back those people and she was murdered to silence her," it added. Rajput mourned her death in an Instagram story. "It's such devastating news. My deepest condolences to Disha's family and friends. May your soul rest in peace," he wrote. In the initial days, Disha's death went largely unnoticed until less than a week later, Rajput himself was found dead in his home. Police also ruled his death to be a case of suicide, saying he had mental health issues for which he was under treatment. But weeks later, his actress girlfriend Rhea Chakraborty was arrested following accusations from Rajput's father that she had contributed to his suicide. He also denied that his son had any mental health issues. Following outrage, Sushant's case was also handed over to the CBI which, last year, closed the case, saying he had indeed died by suicide and that neither Chakraborty nor her family had a role in his death. In the FIR Satish Salian has registered with the CBI, he has alleged that the deaths of Disha and Rajput are linked. Disha, he says, shared with the actor "incriminating and objectionable information concerning alleged drug trafficking, child abuse and other unlawful activities" involving a former minister and some others and the two intended to hold a press conference to bring it into the public domain. "In order to prevent that and protect the persons involved, a well-orchestrated criminal conspiracy was hatched. The victim was gang raped and murdered, and thereafter evidence was suppressed /fabricated and a false story of suicide was created to cover up the crimes and shield the accused." In its order, the court said that registration of the FIR "does not imply any finding of guilt against anyone" and that no-one shall be treated as an accused unless the investigating officer finds "sufficient grounds to raise reasonable suspicion against them". But as the FIR names some of the state's top politicians, police officers and Bollywood actors, the case has dominated headlines in India amid allegations of misuse of political power, denials and claims of political vendetta. Satish Salian, who's been fighting for six years to get justice for his daughter, says he's felt "some peace" after the court ordered the fresh investigation into her death. Disha, he told the BBC, was "very bright, she did well in her studies and read a lot. She had a heart of gold and was very helpful. She was our only child and she loved us very much". His wife, he says, has been unable to come to terms with her tragic death and has gone into depression. "I want the death penalty for those who hurt my daughter. Those who inflicted pain on her must die a painful death too. That is what justice for Disha would look like to me," he says.

item.title: Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4gm7l742dmo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war - Published Ibrahim Issa, 50, is from the Yemeni coastal town of Dhubab, right on the front lines of the war between Yemen's Houthis and the Saudi-backed pro-government forces fighting them. Today he sits, surrounded by his family, on a tarpaulin spread over a sandy floor inside a vast open-sided warehouse at Markazi camp in Obock, northern Djibouti, packed with Yemeni families who have fled by boat across the narrow Bab al-Mandab Strait. After their sea crossing, Yemeni refugees have made their way by truck and on foot to this camp, jointly administered by the government and the UN. "How could I just sit there when my kids are screaming and shaking in terror?" says Ibrahim Issa. "When the sound of the planes start, and the kids hear the planes, they begin shouting and screaming. As parents it is our responsibility, what can you do when you see this? That is why we fled, to save them." - UK to provide Saudi Arabia with 'defensive' military support, says Burnham - Published7 hours ago - Lightning Houthi advance in Yemen may bring dangerous new dimension to Iran war - Published11 September As a fisherman, Ibrahim Issa already owned a boat large enough to bring out his family from Yemen. He even brought several of the family's goats which I can now see nibbling at scraps nearby, foraging amidst the discarded canisters of cooking gas and empty plastic bottles. Some families have been able to bring small bundles of possessions with them from Yemen – one family has even brought a "jeraak", a tall metal shisha pipe – but others have arrived, exhausted, in just the clothes they left in. In just the last few days more than 3,000 refugees have arrived here from Yemen, many entire families. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast. This month, the country's Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen years ago, made a lightning dash down the coast towards Bab al-Mandab, the narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. Saudi Arabia, which backs the internationally recognised government of Yemen, has responded with hundreds of air strikes along the flat, coastal plain where the Houthis are now digging in. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia. "We don't care which side it is that's attacking," is the message I got loud and clear in Arabic from everyone here I spoke to. "It's the bombs falling all around us that have caused us to flee." Djibouti, a tiny former French colony that sits just across the water from Yemen, has made it clear it has no intention of involving itself in the war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government. And yet Djibouti is one of the most militarised nations in Africa. Since 2003, the US has run a huge multinational base here, Camp Lemonnier, once home to the French Foreign Legion. China too has a major base here, its largest military presence on the Indian Ocean and recently upgraded. Back in Markazi camp, one of those I spoke to is Qassim Abraham Abssy. Once also a fisherman, his identity card shows him to be 100 years old. "What led us to come here?" he asks rhetorically. "It was the planes. The sounds of the planes, boom! That's what made us flee, for the sake of our children. It burns ours hearts. We don't know which side they are from. They are bombing everywhere, because the Houthis are everywhere, in the mountains, in the roads. A plane comes, bombs everywhere." Outside in the blazing 37C heat, close to the neat lines of tents supplied by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, I met Mohammed Abdullarim from Aden, a 63-year-old former tour guide old enough to have been born when Aden was still a British protectorate. Unlike the new arrivals, Mohammed has been here since 2015. He fled to Djibouti soon after the fighting first flared up between the Houthis and the government of the now-ousted President Abdrabbuh Mansour Hadi. He has been at the camp ever since but suddenly, as we were talking, the sadness of what is happening to his country overwhelmed him and he turned his head away, choking back tears. "Most of the people here are in the worst condition, inside the tents here. I am very touched, I'm crying for these people, for my people, for their suffering. I want our voices to be heard by the NGOs and the Djibouti government. And I'm thankful to them for accepting us." How long will they have to stay here? That depends, of course, on the fighting. Yemen has been wracked by a horrific civil war that has killed tens of thousands of people and displaced millions since 2014. A shaky, UN-brokered 2022 truce between the Saudis and the Houthis has broken down spectacularly in recent months, with the two sides trading missiles, drones and air strikes. Yemen's war may be a remote one to most people but the effect of choking off Saudi Arabia's oil exports through the Bab al-Mandab Strait are well publicised. But as ever, it is often the human cost that goes unnoticed. Sitting beside his wife on their tarpaulin, amid the cacophony all around them, Qassim Abssy the fisherman is wary of leaving the safety of Djibouti: "If the war continues then we're not going back because we have peace here." His wife, Aisha Abdulkadir Mohammed, agrees. "We are willing to go back in peace if peace returns to our country, and we are praying to God that peace does return. All we need is peace, even for our children's future, they get safety first, then food, water and an education. "As you see we just fled with our clothes, and left everything behind, because [in Yemen] there is no peace." - Published2 days ago - Published4 days ago - Published6 days ago - Published5 days ago

Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important? Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after Iran-backed Houthis seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. Now, following a Saudi request, the UK has said it will deploy a military aircraft to help refuel Saudi Arabian fighter jets taking part in "purely defensive" missions. The BBC's Frank Gardner has this analysis. Inside Djibouti refugee camp for thousands fleeing Houthi advance in Yemen Fighting on Yemen's west coast has prompted thousands of people to flee by boat across the Bab al-Mandab Strait to Djibouti over the last ten days. The BBC's Frank Gardner visited a refugee camp in Obock, a small port town where officials are preparing for the arrival of up to 10,000 refugees. The UN International Organisation for Migration said people were travelling on overcrowded boats and arriving with very limited food and water. The crossings were sparked by an offensive by the Iran-backed Houthi movement to take control of a key island and seize the strategically important port of Mokha.
